author: hmnd
bodyHtml:
Thank you so much for this awesome solution!

For those looking at this in 2024, neovim has changed where they store sockets. Here's an updated version that also supports monorepos:

#!/bin/bash
filename=$1
line=${2:-"1"}
column=${3:-"1"}
#<C-\\><C-N> -> go to normal mode, open file, navigate to correct line and column
command="<C-\\><C-N>:n $filename<CR>:call cursor($line,$column)<CR>"
# nvim default sockets are always nested somewhere in here
# see: https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/7c661207cc4357553ed2b057b6c8f28400024361/src/nvim/msgpack_rpc/server.c#L89
socket_directory="${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR}"
# use find to, well, find them all! (-type s -> socket)
nvim_sockets=($(find "$socket_directory"  -maxdepth 1 -type s -name 'nvim.*'))

for socket in "${nvim_sockets[@]}"
do
   #now it gets nasty... 
   #socket is of shape something.user.pid.count
   #so to get the pid we do this:
   #replace "dots" in socket with linebreaks and return the second to last line (the pid)
   pid=($(echo $socket | tr "." "\n" | tail -n 2))
   echo $pid
   #now we want to get the cwd this process is running in
   #use lsof to get table for this pid, grep row with file descriptor cwd 
   #now replace spaces in row with linebreaks and return the second to last line (the pid)
   pid_cwd=($(lsof -p $pid | grep cwd | tr " " "\n" | tail -n 1))
   #only if process cwd is the same as the pwd, run the command
   if [[  $PWD =~ ^"$pid_cwd"  ]]; then
      nvim --server $socket --remote-send "$command"
   fi
done

author: MikeBellika
bodyHtml:
Thank you for this article, very informative and well written!
I couldn't get this working on mac, I think because it doesn't use XDG_RUNTIME_DIR. I modified the script so it gets the socket directory by calling stdpath and uses that find the sockets. Also made some changes to get it working with my mono repo setup:

Got ChatGPT to go a bit overboard with the comments. Don't really work with bash that often so they're helpful to me

#!/bin/bash
filename="$1"
line_number="${2:-1}"
column_number="${3:-1}"

##############################################################################
# 1. Get the parent process' current working directory.
#    - $PPID references the parent process ID.
#    - We use `lsof` to list the open files for the parent process, filter out
#      the CWD entry, then cut off the first character 'n' that `lsof` returns.
##############################################################################
parent_process_cwd="$(lsof -a -p "$PPID" -d cwd -Fn | grep '^n' | cut -c2-)"

##############################################################################
# 2. Create the command string to be sent to Neovim.
#    - <C-\><C-N> ensures we're in normal mode.
#    - :n opens the file in a new buffer.
#    - :call cursor(line_number, column_number) moves the cursor.
##############################################################################
nvim_command="<C-\\><C-N>:n ${parent_process_cwd}/${filename}<CR>:call cursor(${line_number},${column_number})<CR>"

##############################################################################
# 3. Get Neovim’s base runtime directory.
#    - We run Neovim in headless mode to print the parent directory of the
#      runtime path, then exit.
##############################################################################
base_runtime_dir="$(nvim --headless -c "lua print((vim.fn.stdpath('run'):match('^(.+)/')))" -c "q" 2>&1)"

##############################################################################
# 4. Find all potential Neovim sockets in the base runtime directory.
#    - These socket files have names like 'nvim.<PID>.0'.
##############################################################################
nvim_sockets=($(find "$base_runtime_dir" -type s -name 'nvim.*'))

##############################################################################
# 5. Identify the socket that best matches our current working directory.
#    - We'll track the "most specific" match by counting the number of
#      directory separators '/' in the socket's working directory.
##############################################################################
best_match_socket=""
best_match_depth=0

for socket in "${nvim_sockets[@]}"; do
  # Extract the PID (process ID) from the socket name.
  pid="$(echo "$socket" | tr '.' '\n' | tail -n 2 | head -n 1)"

  # Retrieve the working directory for the socket's process.
  socket_cwd="$(lsof -a -p "$pid" -d cwd -Fn | grep '^n' | cut -c2-)"

  # If the socket's working directory matches our current PWD (prefix match),
  # calculate how deep it is by counting the number of '/' characters.
  if [[ -n "$socket_cwd" && -n "$PWD" && "$PWD" =~ ^"$socket_cwd" ]]; then
    socket_depth="$(echo "$socket_cwd" | tr -cd '/' | wc -c)"
    if ((socket_depth > best_match_depth)); then
      best_match_depth=$socket_depth
      best_match_socket=$socket
    fi
  fi
done

##############################################################################
# 6. Send the command to the best matched Neovim server, if found.
##############################################################################
if [[ -n "$best_match_socket" ]]; then
  nvim --server "$best_match_socket" --remote-send "$nvim_command"
else
  echo "No matching Neovim server found."
fi

author: nasso
bodyHtml:
hey, thanks everyone for all the tips!

to make it easier for myself to setup on new machines, and also for the meme, i Rewrote-it-in-Rust 🚀 🦀 : https://tangled.org/nasso.dev/launch-editor-nvim/

if you have Cargo, all you have to do is:

cargo install --locked launch-editor-nvim
echo "export LAUNCH_EDITOR=launch-editor-nvim" > ~/.zshenv # or wherever you put your env vars

it includes all the shiny tweaks by @hmnd and @MikeBellika:

  • tested to work on most recent neovim (i have v0.11.5)
  • calls vim.fn.stdpath('run') in a headless nvim to find the path to the sockets in a portable way
  • selects the neovim instance for which the cwd is the closest ancestor to the file being open (this is to "support monorepos")
  • bonus by me: i tweaked the vim command to make it a single "jump"; <C-O> will go back to the previous file, rather than the position you were in the file before setting the cursor position

i did this mostly for fun, but it could probably also be made cross-platform and support windows too! shouldn't be too hard; patches welcome :3
